A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, Identifiable Equivariant Networks are Layerwise Equivariant. Their text, equations, figures, and Appendices A–C support reliable comparison. The appendices are unchanged apart from pagination.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 2–3 report original experiments showing learned filters and attention patterns in CIFAR10-trained MLPs and an attention autoencoder.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds quantitative measurements of learned equivariance in Section 6.1 and Table 1.

M1.justification: The MLP and attention architectures, training objectives, and equivariance losses are unchanged. The newly introduced least-squares fitting of latent transformations is an evaluation procedure applied to existing networks.

E1.justification: Section 6.1 adds evaluation on synthetic noise inputs and an up-down-mirroring scenario beyond the trained left-right symmetry. CIFAR10, autoencoding, and classification remain the underlying training coverage.

E2.justification: No comparison method is added or removed. Table 1 evaluates the same Tanh and GELU autoencoder/classifier variants already compared qualitatively in Figure 2; up-down mirroring is an evaluation control.

E3.justification: The new diagnostic fits linear transformations using 100,000 noise samples and evaluates median relative equivariance error on 100,000 independent noise samples. It tests representations through the first nonlinearity and through the second linear layer, under both mirror directions. Existing training settings in Appendix C are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 supplements the existing visual case studies with a focused quantitative analysis of representation depth, activation choice, and trained versus untrained mirroring symmetry. This tests whether the visual patterns correspond to approximate linear equivariance.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table 1 aggregates per-input errors using medians without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds 16 equivariance-error measurements. For example, the GELU autoencoder has left-right errors of 0.40 after the first nonlinearity and 0.11 after the second linear layer; every left-right error is below its corresponding up-down error. These are new diagnostics, not performance gains over v1. Existing visual results are retained.

T1.justification: The formal definitions, Theorem 4.1, its Appendix A proof, and the Appendix B example are unchanged. Conjecture 5.1 and Corollary 5.3 retain the same assertion about equivalent weakly identifiable representatives. Added explanations and applicability qualifications supply no new formal result or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the central claim that equivariance and suitable identifiability imply layerwise equivariance. The abstract formalism, applications to MLPs and attention networks, and empirical illustrations remain the stated contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly identifies possible adjunction failures for Deep Sets and equivariant graph networks, and cautions that ReLU may require larger symmetry groups or submodels. It distinguishes approximate experimental equivariance from the exact theory and states that the existential theorem does not explain optimization dynamics. The new measurements also extend the interpretation of GELU cancellation across two linear layers.

D1.justification: Section 6.1 documents the new analysis's least-squares fitting, evaluated layer compositions, sample counts, independent evaluation samples, and error aggregation. Appendix C's hardware, architecture dimensions, preprocessing, and training hyperparameters remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references on identifiability and equivariant approximation, including Massarenti and Mella, Grillo and Montúfar, Hendi et al., Dym and Maron, and Cen et al. Deep Sets and equivariant graph networks are newly cited to discuss applicability boundaries. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: Targeted additions explain group actions and submodels, revise the conjecture's wording, and clarify experimental aims and limitations. An Impact Statement and conference publication information are added. The section organization and appendix exposition are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Table 1 and repositions Figure 3 beneath it, with accompanying text reflow. Figures 1–3 retain the same image content and captions, and the appendix diagrams remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: Table 1 strengthens the previously visual empirical support with quantitative measurements on independent evaluation inputs and an untrained-mirroring control. The added architectural, approximation, and optimization caveats make the theory's scope clearer. These are useful, bounded improvements; the main theorem, proof, and original experiments remain unchanged.
